## Methods

Animal care and mouse strains
Animal studies were conducted in the accredited SPF animal facility in the CAM-SU Genomic Resource Center and approved by the Animal Care and Use Committee of CAM-SU under a protocol of ZJ-2021-1 approved on 12/24/2021. Mice were maintained at room temperature (23–25°C) when indicated with a 12 h light/dark cycle (illuminated from 8:00) and free access to acidified water and radiated and autoclaved food unless specified. All mice were maintained on a C57BL/6N background. C57BL/6N-Slc25a1tm1c(EUCOMM)Wtsi/Cmsu were obtained by injecting mutant mouse ES cells into mouse blastocysts CAM-SU Genomic Resource Center. The Adipocyte-specific deletion of Slc25a1 was generated by breeding Adiponectin-Cre (stock #010803) and Slc25a1-flox/flox mice. The pups were identified by PCR followed by sequence analysis using primers (Cre-F: ACGGACAGAAGCATTTTCCA; Cre-R: GGATGTGCCATGTGAGTCTG; flox-F: GGAAGGCAATCCTAGCAGGTGGGTC; flox-R: CAGCTGCGTCTTCACGTATTCGGTC).

Wild type male C57BL/6N were obtained from CAM-SU Genomic Resource Center. For fasting experiments, male C57BL/6N (10–12 weeks of age) were divided into three groups: ad libitum and fasted (12 h or 36 h). The fasted group fasted for 12 h or 36 h, began at ZT12, and were sacrificed at ZT0 with the ad libitum group. For fasting and refeeding experiments, male C57BL/6N (10–12 weeks of age) were divided into two groups: fasted and refed. The fasted group fasted for 36 h, and the refed group fasted for 36 h and then refed the chow diet for 3–6 h before the study.

Human samples
Visceral adipose tissues from individuals with different BMIs were surgically collected from the Second Affiliated Hospital of Soochow University under a protocol of JD-LK-2020-038-01 approved by the Ethics Community of the Second Affiliated Hospital of Soochow University. Human serum was isolated from venous blood collection under standard procedures from the Second Affiliated Hospital of Soochow University. The signed informed consent has been collected from all participants.

Quantitation of ADMA in human plasma samples
Human plasma samples were extracted with an extraction solvent containing internal standards (40 ng/mL d7-ADMA). The whole extraction process was the same as for drug analysis. The ADMA standard curve was made by dissolving the standard to a series concentration using 5% BSA as a surrogate matrix. Standards d7-ADMA (purity: 98%) were purchased from Cambridge Isotope Laboratories (Tewksbury, MA, USA), and ADMA (purity: 98%) from targetMOl (Boston, MA, USA).

UPLC separation was performed using a Shimadzu Nexera X2 liquid chromatography system with a binary gradient pump, autosampler (4°C), and column oven (40°C) for chromatographic separation. A hydrophilic interaction liquid chromatographic column (HILIC, 150 × 2.1 mm, 1.7 µm, Atlantis, Waters) was applied for separation. The injection volume was 2 µL. A binary eluent system was used at a flow rate of 0.3 mL/min. Mobile phase A was an aqueous buffer containing 10 mM ammonium formate, and 0.1% formic acid, and mobile phase B was acetonitrile with 0.1% formic acid. The programmed gradient was 0-0.5 min: 90% B, 0.5–1 min: 90% to 70% B, 1–6 min: 70% to 65% B, 6–6.5 min: 65%-40% B, 6.5-7.5 min: 40% B, 7.5–8 min: 40%-90% B, 8-9 min: 90% B. Multiple reaction monitoring (MRM) data acquisition mode (for ADMA: 203.1–46.3) were performed on an AB Sciex 6500 QTrap® hybrid triple quadrupole/linear ion trap mass spectrometer with IonDrive™ Turbo V ion source and ESI probe. Spectra were obtained in ESI+ under the following conditions: curtain gas 35 psi, ion spray voltage (IS) 5500 V, the pressure of ion source gas 1 55 psi, ion source gas 2 55 psi, declustering potential 60 V, entrance potential 10 V, and collision cell exit potential 10 V. Data collection and quantification were carried out by SCIEX Analyst and SCIEX OS, respectively.

Feeding schedule and diets
For all high-fat diets (HFD, XTHF60, Xietong Pharmaceutical Bioengineering) feeding experiments, mice began dietary intervention at 6–8 weeks old with a body weight of ~25 g. Under 16:8 TRF, mice were allowed access to food between ZT13 (9 p.m.) and ZT21 (5 a.m.). Food access was regulated by transferring mice daily between cages with food and water and cages with water only. As a control, ad-lib-fed mice were also transferred between feeding cages at the same time.

For NRF and DRF, mice were allowed access to food between nighttime (8 p.m. to 8 a.m.) or daytime (8 a.m. to 8 p.m.) for one month, separately.

Drug treatments
SGC707 (S7832, PRMT3 inhibitor), CTPI-2 (S2968, SLC25A1 inhibitor) and MK-2206 2HCL (S1078, AKT1/2/3 kinase inhibitor) were purchased from MaoKang Biotechnology. For prevention or reversion phenotypes of mice fed an HFD, SGC707 was administered at 10 mg/kg or 30 mg/kg via intraperitoneal injection on alternated days, respectively.

SGC707 was diluted in DMSO (at 5% final concentration), and DMSO served as the vehicle control.

For MK-2206 treated experiments, MK-2206 was diluted in DMSO (at 5% final concentration) and administered at 50 mg/kg via intraperitoneal injection, with DMSO serving as a vehicle control.

Drug analysis by using HPLC-MS/MS
The drug was fully dissolved in methanol at 1 µg/mL for HPLC-MSMS analysis. The drug compounds in mice tissue samples were first extracted with methanol and acetonitrile (1:9, v/v). After thorough vortex and ultrasonication, the samples were centrifuged (×18,000 g, 4°C for 15 min) to extract the supernatants. Following vacuum dryness (Savant SPD2010, Thermo scientific), the residues were redissolved in acetonitrile and H2O (1:1, v/v) for further analysis. All analytical chemicals, including formic acid (Honeywell), methanol (Macklin), acetonitrile (Fisher) and H2O (ThermoFisher) used in the analysis were MS-grade.

The extracts were analyzed using HPLC-QTOF MS/MS (1290II-6530C, Agilent) equipped with a Thermo Hypersil GOLD aQ C18 column (2.1 × 100 mm, 1.9 μm) with a 24 min gradient. Flow rate 0.4 ml/min, Column temperature 40°C. MS-grade water with 0.1% formic acid (v/v) was used as mobile phase A, and MS-grade ACN with 0.1% formic acid (v/v) was used as mobile phase B. The gradient started at 5% B, keep 1 min, gradually increased to 55% B at 12 min, and to 100% B at 17 min and maintained until 20 min, then reverted to the initial condition of 5% at 22 min and then held at 5% to 24 min. Sample analysis was conducted in positive ionization mode (ESI+) and collected in full-scan and targeted MS/MS modes, respectively. The nitrogen temperature of the ion source was set to 250°C, the dry gas 10 L/min, the nebulizer 45 psi, the sheath gas temperature 350°C, the sheath gas flow rate 11 L/min, the nozzle voltage 1000 V, the Vcap 4000 V, the fragmentor 100 V, the skimmer 45 V, and the detection window 20 ppm. For targeted MS/MS analysis, the collision energy was set to 20 eV.

Data was collected by Agilent data acquisition software in centroid mode. The Masshunter quantitative analysis software from the vendor was further used to extract the targeted ion chromatogram and MSMS spectra and to calculate the retention time, peak areas, signal-to-noise ratio, etc.

HEK293T, primary adipocyte and porcine adipocyte culture
HEK293T cells (CRL-3216, ATCC) were grown in Dulbecco’s modified eagle medium (DMEM)/high glucose with 10% fetal bovine serum (FBS) as well as 100 μ/mL penicillin and 100 μg/mL streptomycin (15140-122, Gibco). All cell lines were maintained under standard conditions (37°C, 5% CO2).

For primary adipocyte culture, subcutaneous and epididymal adipose tissues from 6- to 8-week-old mice were minced into small pieces, followed by incubation with 1.25 mg/mL Collagenase from Clostridium histolyticum (C0130-5G, Sigma-Aldrich) in DMEM containing Penicillin/Streptomycin for 40–50 min in a 37°C shaker water bath. Cell suspension buffer was filtered through a 100 μm cell strainer and centrifugated for 10 min at 700×g to get the stromal vascular fraction pellet. For white adipocyte differentiation, the stromal vascular fraction was cultured in DMEM complete medium to 90–95% confluence and then differentiated in DMEM complete medium containing (0.64 μM dexamethasone, 0.625 mM IBMX, 1.6 μg/ml insulin and 1 μM rosiglitazone) for 4 days, change medium every 2 days. Cells were then changed to DMEM complete medium containing 1.6 μg/ml insulin every 2 days until more than 90% of cells were fully differentiated to mature adipocytes before the following experiment. Insulin (PB180432) was obtained from Pricella Biotechnology; Dexamethasone (D4902), 3-isobutyl-methylxanthine (410957, IBMX), Rosiglitazone (557366-M) and 3,3’,5-Triiodo-L-thyronine (T2877, T3) were purchased from Sigma-Aldrich.

Immortalized porcine white pre-adipocytes were cultured in growth medium containing Dulbecco’s modification of Eagle’s medium (DMEM), 15% FBS (Gibco), 1% penicillin/streptomycin (Invitrogen) at 37°C with 5% CO2. For porcine white adipocytes, adipogenic differentiation, the cells were induced with induction medium (IM) containing DMEM, 10% FBS (Gibco), 500 μM 3-isobutylmethylxanthine (Yeasen Biotechnology Co., Ltd.), 5 μg/mL insulin (WISENT Inc.), 1 μg/mL rosiglitazone (Yeasen Biotechnology Co., Ltd.), and 1 μM dexamethasone (Yeasen Biotechnology Co., Ltd.) for 3 days and then differentiated in differentiation medium (DM) contains DMEM, 10% FBS and 5 μg/mL insulin for 2 days.

Histological analysis
Mice were anesthetised with isoflurane and then euthanasia via cervical dislocation, and adipose and liver tissues were harvested and fixed with 4% paraformaldehyde. Paraffin embedding, tissue sectioning, and hematoxylin and eosin staining were performed.

Total RNA extraction and real-time PCR
Mice were anesthetized with isoflurane, and then euthanasia via cervical dislocation and tissue samples were collected and frozen with liquid nitrogen. Total RNA was extracted from cells or tissues by using Trizol Reagent (15596026, Invitrogen) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. Synthesis of cDNA was performed using 1 μg total RNA from each sample using HiScript IV Reverse Transcriptase (R423-01, vazyme). Quantitative PCR (qPCR) was carried out using the ChamQ Universal SYBR qPCR Master Mix (Q711, vazyme) and analyzed on a QuantStudio 3 Real-Time PCR System (Thermo Fisher Scientific). Primer sequences were obtained from PrimerBank.

Transcriptome sequencing
Total RNA was extracted according to the instructions manual of the TRlzol Reagent (Life Technologies, California, USA). RNA concentration and purity were measured using NanoDrop 2000 (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Wilmington, DE). RNA integrity was assessed using the RNA Nano 6000 Assay Kit of the Agilent Bioanalyzer 2100 system (Agilent Technologies, CA, USA). A total amount of 1 μg RNA per sample was used as input material for the RNA sample preparations. Sequencing libraries were generated using the NEBNext Ultra TM RNA Library Prep Kit for Illumina (NEB, USA), following the manufacturer’s recommendations. Index codes were added to attribute sequences to each sample. Briefly, mRNA was purified from total RNA using poly-T oligo-attached magnetic beads. Fragmentation was carried out using divalent cations under elevated temperature in NEBNext First Strand Synthesis Reaction Buffer (5X. First-strand cDNA was synthesized using a random hexamer primer and M-MuLV Reverse Transcriptase. Second-strand cDNA synthesis was subsequently performed using DNA Polymerase I and RNase H. Remaining overhangs were converted into blunt ends via exonuclease/polymerase activities. After adenylation of 3’ ends of DNA fragments, NEBNext Adapter with hairpin loop structure was ligated to prepare for hybridization. In order to select cDNA fragments of preferentially 240 bp in length, the library fragments were purified with the AMPure XP system (Beckman Colter, Beverly, USA). Then 3 μl USER Enzyme (NEB, USA) was used with size-selected, adaptor-ligated cDNA at 37°C for 15 min followed by 5 min at 95°C before PCR. Then, PCR was performed using Phusion High-Fidelity DNA polymerase, Universal PCR primers, and Index (X) Primer. Finally, PCR products were purified (AMPure XP system), and library quality was assessed using the Agilent Bioanalyzer 2100 system. The clustering of the index-coded samples was performed on a cBot Cluster Generation System using TruSeq PE Cluster Kit v4-cBot-HS (Illumia) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. After cluster generation, the library preparations were sequenced on an Illumina platform and paired-end reads were generated.

Immunoprecipitation
The cells were collected and suspended in 1000 μL lysis buffer (1% Nonidet P-40, 1 mM EDTA, 150 mM NaCl in 50 mM Tris-HCL, pH 7.5) containing protease inhibitors cocktail (B14001, Bimake) and phosphatase inhibitors cocktail (B15001, Bimake), then passed 12 times through a 22G needle followed by centrifugation at 12,000×g for 10 min at 4°C. Eighty microlitres of supernatants mixed with membrane solubilization buffer plus the 5× loading buffer as the input sample. 800 μL of supernatants were immunoprecipitated with beads conjugated with the indicated antibodies at 4°C for 6–8 h. After incubation, the beads were washed four times with a lysis buffer, and the precipitates were eluted with 5× loading buffer. Elutes and whole-cell extracts were resolved on SDS-PAGE, followed by a western blot with the indicated antibodies. The following plasmids were constructed by standard molecular cloning technics: pcDNA3.1-PRMT3-MYC encodes full-length human PRMT3 followed by MYC epitope tag, pCMV-PRMT3-HA encodes full-length mouse PRMT3 followed by HA epitope tag, pcDNA3.1-PRMT5-MYC encodes full-length human PRMT5 followed by MYC epitope tag, pCGN-SLC25A1-Flag encodes full-length mouse SLC25A1 followed by Flag epitope tag.

Immunoblotting
Mice were anesthetized with isoflurane, and then euthanasia via cervical dislocation and tissue samples were collected and frozen with liquid nitrogen. Cells or tissues were collected and homogenized in the RIPA buffer (1% Nonidet P-40, 0.1% SDS, 1 mM EDTA, 150 mM NaCl in 50 mM Tris-HCL, pH 7.5) supplemented with protease inhibitor cocktail and phosphatase inhibitors cocktail. The protein concentrations of lysates were determined using the BCA method (A55864, Thermo Fisher Scientific). The equal amounts of total proteins were resolved by SDS–PAGE and transferred to PVDF membranes (IPVH00010, Merck Millipore). Immunoblots were blocked with 5% non-fat milk (1172GR500, BioFroxx) in Tris-buffered saline (TBS) containing 0.01% Tween 20 (TBST), probed with indicated primary antibodies overnight at 4°C. After washing in TBST three times, blots were incubated with horseradish peroxidase-conjugated secondary antibodies diluted in TBST supplemented with 5% skim milk for 1 h at room temperature and followed by at least 3 washes with TBST. Immunoreactivity was developed with enzymatic detection using SuperPico ECL Chemiluminescence Kit (E422, E423, Vazyme).

Primary antibodies used for immunoblots were as follows: anti-Mono-Methyl Arginine (8015, MMA, diluted 1:1000), Asymmetric Di-Methyl Arginine Motif (13522, ADMA, diluted 1:1000), Symmetric Di-Methyl Arginine Motif (13222, SDMA, diluted 1:1000), Normal anti-rabbit lgG (2729), Normal anti-mouse lgG (68860), Phospho-Akt (Ser473) (4060, diluted 1:1000), AKT (9272, diluted 1:1000), PRMT4 (3379, diluted 1:1000), PRMT5 (79998, diluted 1:1000), PKM1/2 (3106, diluted 1:1000), Pyruvate Carboxylase (49381, PC, diluted 1:1,000), LDHA (2012, diluted 1:1000), CPT2 (52552, diluted 1:1000), PGK1 (63536, diluted 1:1000), PCK1 (12940, diluted 1:1000), Phospho-HSL (Ser660) (45804, diluted 1:1000) antibodies were purchased from Cell Signaling technology. Anti-ATGL (55190-1-AP, diluted 1:1000), HSL (17333-1-AP, diluted 1:1000), HSP90 (13171-1-AP, diluted 1:1000), PRMT3 (17628-1-AP, diluted 1:1000), Beta Actin (66009-1-Ig, diluted 1:1000), GAPDH (60004-1-Ig, diluted 1:1000), Alpha Tubulin (66031-1-Ig, diluted 1:5000), SLC25A1 (15235-1-AP, diluted 1:1000) antibodies were obtained from Proteintech. Anti-FLAG-M2 (F1804, diluted 1:5000), FLAG (SAB4301135, diluted 1:5000), HA (H6908, diluted 1:5000), FLAG (H3663, diluted 1:5000), MYC (C3956, diluted 1:5000), MYC (M4439, diluted 1:5000) antibodies were purchased from Sigma. Horseradish peroxidase-conjugated goat anti-mouse (115-035-003, diluted 1:5000) and anti-rabbit (711-035-152, diluted 1:5000) secondary antibodies were from Jackson ImmunoResearch Laboratories.

Glucose and insulin tolerance test
Glucose and insulin tolerance tests (GTT, ITT) were performed by an intraperitoneal injection of glucose (2 g/kg body weight), insulin (0.03 μg/kg body weight) in mice following 14 hours fasting (for GTT) or 6 hours fasting (for ITT). Blood was collected from a small incision from the tip of the tail before injection (Time 0), then 15, 30, 60, 90 and 120 min after injection of glucose or insulin. Blood glucose levels were measured by a blood glucose meter (Accu-Chek® Active, Roche).

Indirect calorimetry and body composition measurement
The oxygen consumption (VO2) and carbon dioxide production (VCO2) of the mice were measured using an indirect calorimetry system (Oxymax, Columbus Instruments). The system was kept at a stable environmental temperature (24°C) that also had a 12 h light (8 AM-8 PM) and a 12 h dark cycle (8 PM-8 AM). Mice were individually placed in each chamber with free access to food and water. Mice were adapted to the chamber for 24 h before the measurements. The data were presented as uncorrected energy expenditure levels. Average energy expenditure of day (8 AM-8 PM) and night (8 PM-8 AM) values were the average mean value of all points measured during the 12 h. Total body fat and lean mass in live animals without anesthesia were measured by using a Minispec LF50 body composition analyzer located in the Small Animal Facility of CAM-SU. Animals were placed in a specially sized, clear plastic holder without sedation or anesthesia. The holder was then inserted into a tubular space on the side of the Minispec LF50 system. The animals were forced to not move in the holder to guarantee the accuracy of the results. Each scan took about 2 minutes.

Blood biochemistry
Blood biochemistry was performed by using a clinical chemistry analyzer (Hitachi 7100). An appropriate volume of blood that was required (160–200 μl of plasma) for the test was collected from each mouse (mice were anesthetized with isoflurane) and transferred to a gel tube containing lithium Heparin and centrifuge for 15 minutes at 5000×g in a refrigerated centrifuge set at 4°C. If plasma samples cannot be analyzed immediately, keep them at −80°C before analysis. Use plasma samples undiluted or diluted to a ratio of 1:2 with deionised water if the volume was insufficient.

Targeted metabolomics
Collected samples use a liquid mass platform (UPLC-TQ-MS) to detect energy metabolism-related metabolites in biological (Metabo-Profile, Shanghai, P. R. China). The solvents used were chromatographic grade methanol, acetonitrile, and formic acid, which were purchased from Merck Chemicals, Germany. The experimental ultrapure water was prepared by the Millipore Reference ultrapure water system (Billerica, MA, USA) equipped with a 0.22 μm filter head for LC/MS. Before processing the sample, the sample needs to be thawed in an ice bath to reduce sample degradation. Weigh 10 mg tissue into a 1.5 mL EP tube, add 20 μL ultrapure water and 10 magnetic beads, homogenize for 3 min (BB24, Next Advance, Inc., Averill Park, NY, USA), and then add 120 μL pre-cooling. The methanol solution containing internal standard was homogenized again for 3 min. Centrifuge at 18000×g for 20 min at 4°C (Microfuge 20R, Beckman Colter, Inc., Indianapolis, IN, USA), take 100 μL the supernatant in a 1.5 mL EP tube, and concentrate at 4°C (Labconco, Kansas City, MO, USA), add 100 μL 80% methanol solution for reconstitution, centrifuge and transfer to 96-well plate, waiting for sample injection analysis. An ultra-high pressure liquid chromatography-triple quadrupole mass spectrometer (ACQUITY-IUPLC/Xevo TQ-S) from Waters Corporation was used to detect energy metabolism-related metabolites. The raw data generated by UPLC-TQ-MS will use Waters MassLynx software (v4.1, Waters, Milford, MA, USA) for peak extraction, integration, identification and quantitative analysis of each metabolite. Self-developed iMAP software (V1.0, Metabo-Profile, Shanghai, China) is used for subsequent statistical analysis, such as PCA, OPLS-DA and one-dimensional statistical testing.

Measurement of ECAR
ECAR of CTPI-2 (S2968, SLC25A1 inhibitor) and SGC707 treated adipocytes were analyzed using an XF96 Analyzer (Seahorse Bioscience). In brief, 2×104 cells per well were plated in Seahorse XF96 plates in 200 μl of DMEM supplemented with 2 mM glutamine. The plates were incubated for 1 h at 37°C in a humidified incubator without CO2. After assessing the ECAR at baseline, the following compounds were sequentially added to the analyzer, and the change in ECAR was measured: (1) after the addition of 10 mM glucose; (2) after the sequential addition of 1 μM oligomycin and (3) after the sequential addition of 50 mM 2-DG. In this assay, maximum ECAR occurs after the addition of oligomycin. All ECAR measures were performed three times in a mix–wait–measure cycle of 3, 2, and 3 min, respectively. Rotenone (S2348), 2-Deoxy-D-glucose (S4701, 2-DG), Oligomycin A (S1478) and Indomethacin (S1723) from Selleck Chemicals; Antimycin A (MS0070) were obtained from Shanghai MaoKang Biotechnology, China.

Statistical analysis
Data analysis was conducted mainly in Prism 8.0.1. The rhythmicity of gene expression was evaluated using JTK analysis, with a p-value of <0.05 indicative of rhythmicity. All analyses were conducted using the Student’s t test (two-tail). All experimental data were presented as mean ± SEM. Comparisons with P-values <0.05, <0.01 or <0.001 were considered statistically significant.

## Your Original Review (Round 1)

### Reviewer 1

In this manuscript, Huang et al. investigated how dietary conditions, such as time-restricted fasting (TRF) and diet-induced obesity (DIO), affect protein arginine methylation and how mitigation of PRMT activity impacts the metabolic flexibility of the fat tissues. Specifically, they focus on the role of PRMT3 in the visceral adipose tissue (vWAT) of mice. First, they observed that the global arginine methylation level fluctuates in correlation with the feeding cycle and higher methylation levels are observed in mice fed with high-fat diet and in obese individuals. Second, they selectively focus on PRMT3, whose expression pattern mirrors the methylation changes, and showed that inhibiting PRMT3 activity, using a small molecule inhibitor SGC807, reduces DIO by enhancing adipocyte glycolysis. Along this line, they also revealed that the insulin-AKT signaling pathway acts upstream to regulate the levels of PRMT3 protein expression and arginine methylation. Third, they focus on SLC25A1, a citrate transporter located in the mitochondria, and showed that SLC25A1 interacts with PRMT3 and likely is methylated by PRMT3 and that its expression also follows the pattern of the feeding cycle. Fourth, they demonstrated that time-restricted fasting together with PRMT3 inhibition greatly reduces diet-induced obesity. Lastly, they showed that adipocyte-specific deletion of SLC25A1 could reduce high fat-diet induced obesity by enhancing glucose metabolism, indicating that modulating SLC25A1 expression, maybe through PRMT3-mediated pathway, could promote adipocyte glucose metabolism and prevent diet-induced obesity.
Overall, this manuscript made a few interesting observations, such as 1) global changes of arginine methylation in response to the feeding cycle; 2) mitigating of HFD-induced obesity by small molecule inhibitor SGC707; 3) correlation of SLC25A1 expression with the feeding cycle; and 4) reduction of HFD-induced obesity by adipocyte-specific knockout of SLC25A1. Although these individual conclusions seem to be well supported by data, they are not logically connected due to the lack of mechanisms. At this stage, the manuscript is deemed too descriptive and preliminary.
Major critiques:
1. Regarding the global changes of arginine methylation in response to feeding. The authors suggest that changes in PRMT3 protein level are the cause. However, this conclusion is not well supported: 1) gene expression changes under the feeding cycle, fasting, and high-fat diet could contribute to the changes of methylation signal on western blot gel. It might not be related to altered methylation on a given protein. 2) PRMT1 is the major PRMT that catalyzes more than 90% of ADMA, however, it was excluded at the very beginning of this study. The authors mentioned a similar study (it was not cited), which reported a strong induction of PRMT1 upon HFD. They should determine the extent to which the alternation of global arginine methylation is contributed by PRMT1 vs PRMT3. 3) PRMT3 has only a few reported substrates. It is unlikely that PRMT3 is responsible for global methylation changes. In addition to using SGC707, they should also knockdown or knockout PRMT3 in eWAT to complement the results with the inhibitor. 4) The alternation of certain metabolites involved in the methylation pathway could lead to tissue-specific and global changes of methylation. Because the feeding cycle, fasting, and high-fat diet could have significant impacts on metabolism, this possibility should be tested.
2. How PRMT3 expression is regulated by the insulin-AKT pathway is not clear. The authors implicate that PRMT3 could be phosphorylated, although the data supporting this claim is weak. This needs to be thoroughly characterized, such as by which kinase, at which site, what is the impact of methylation. Additionally, if insulin elevates PRMT3 expression, what is its impact on methylation? Does it restore methylation under fasting or in the presence of SGC707?
3. The impact of PRMT3 inhibition, specifically by the small molecule inhibitor SGC707, on lipid metabolism has been reported. This study was not cited or discussed (https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-021-04524-w). Importantly, although the specificity of SGC707 was initially characterized against other methyltransferases in vitro, its specificity in vivo is not clear. The in vivo study using SGC707 (Fig. 3) should be complemented with adipocyte-specific PRMT3 knockout.
4. Regarding the regulation of SLC25A1 by PRMT3. The expression pattern of SLC25A1 in response to the feeding cycle is interesting. Although this change mirrors the changes of PRMT3, whether there is a direct causative relationship is not addressed. Also, the rationale for focusing on SLC25A1 as the downstream target of PRMT3 is not strong. They mentioned a previous publication regarding SLC25A1 interaction with PRMT3 and PRMT5. This paper was not cited. The authors suggest that PRMT3 might methylate SLC25A1 or at least regulate SCL25A1 methylation. This needs to be thoroughly characterized, including the sites of methylation on SLC25A1, and how methylation may directly affect SLC25A1 protein level. Additionally, the authors suggest that SLC25A1 expression is also regulated by the insulin-AKT pathway (Fig. 4p). Is this through PRMT3? Lastly, what contributes to the tissue-specific regulation of PRMT3 and SLC25A1 in eWAT, but not in other adipose tissues?
5. Although PRMT3 inhibition by SGC707 and adipocyte-specific knockout of SLC25A1 both reduce diet-induced obesity, the extent to which PRMT3-mediated SLC25A1 methylation contributes to this process is not clear. For example, will supplement the expression of SLC25A1 in PRMT3 KO restores some of the metabolic features? Similarly, what happens if applying SGC707 on SCL25A1 conditional knockout mouse model? It is more convincing that SLC25A1 expression changes in response to feeding, whereas changes in PRMT3 are rather minor.
6. Page 9, section title “TRF reduces PRMT3-SLC25A1 interaction…” was not supported by the data shown in Fig. 5.
Other critiques
1. The authors use recombinant proteins to test the specificity of PRMT3 antibody. This method is not appropriate. They should use PRMT3 knockout cell lines to confirm that the signal they see with the antibody is indeed PRMT3 (PRMT3 knockout cells are viable). In many cases, the changes of PRMT3 protein levels are very marginal (eg. Fig. 2b, 2f, 2j, 2l, Fig. 3r, Fig. 5a).
2. The correlation between methylation levels and BMI is weak.

### Reviewer 2

In this manuscript the authors study how different dietary approaches change levels of PRMT3 and MMA/ADMA in white adipose tissue (WAT). In WAT, the authors firstly show a circadian regulation of MMA/ADMA levels, which seems to be abrogated upon HFD. Furthermore, inhibition of PRMT3 by SGC707 reverts weight gain on a HFD as well as it accelerates the decrease of MMA/ADMA levels during a 12h fast to levels similar to a 36h fast, on an insulin dependant way. The authors also claim that SLC25a1 is implicated. Besides the role of PRMT3 in the levels of MMA/ADMA, the authors study the changes in these proteins using a Time Restricted Feeding (TRF) paradigm and draw a parallel between TRF and SGC707 action upon long term HFD consumption.
Former studies have implicated PRMT3/SGC707 in weight loss and ameliorated phenotype from liver steatosis, also showing an improvement on overall WAT morphology. Overall, literature on PRMT3 or its inhibitor is lacking in models of HFD, and its effects on body weight, although known, are still quite understudied. This adds to the novelty of this present study.
Regarding the study itself, in my opinion, some major considerations are as follows:
1. In figure 1c the authors claim that animals on HFD showed a “marked increase” in proteins containing MMA and ADMA. HFD feeding is known to alter several parameters that have a circadian component to it as well as feeding patterns. As such, one can wonder whether the time of collecting the tissue can have an impact on MMA and ADMA levels, and whether repeating the experiment done on figure 1a would help to get a better understanding on whether this changes in protein level are continuous during a 24h period or shifted in comparison to NCD. In my opinion, this experiment has relevance towards the claim of the paper, since understanding the dynamics of protein levels both in NCD as in HFD could influence the timing of fasting for improved outcomes.
2. In figure 2, the authors show that a 12h fast in addition to the administration of SGC mimics the results of a 36h fasting, regarding MMA and ADMA levels. This experiment is central to the claim of the paper, since one of the main premisses is that by inhibiting PRMT3 during a 12h the observed decrease in MMA and ADMA levels is similar to a 36h fast. It is of my opinion that is highly important to also show that, in this particular experiment (figure 2h and 2i) the levels of ADMA and MMA in ad libitum animals administered the drug remain unchanged. In this way its possible to ensure that proper controls are in place.
3. The authors present data on the effects of PRMT3 inhibition in overall metabolism and body mass. The authors claim that no changes in food intake nor energy expenditure were observed on a 24h period. 24h readings can be misleading as small incremental changes can be observed when measures are taking for extended periods of time. A prolonged measurement entailing 5-7 days would allow for a better overview and a more convincing claim that the weight loss is not due to small cumulative changes in feeding amounts/energy expenditure. A longer assessment of the RER could also provide better proof that this delta RER changes are repeated daily in prolonged periods and not on a particular single isolated event.
4. It has been published that TRF changes body weight without affecting total caloric intake, and the authors are able to replicate this finding. Furthermore, in figure S9m, we can observe an increase in locomotion during the night cycle, which also goes with current literature. In this present study, we observe changes in body weight in HFD animals under a TRF paradigm, without alteration of food intake or energy expenditure (Figure S9). It would be important for the authors to adress this particular data set, where increased locomotion but unchanged energy expenditure and feeding behaviour are observed. An important suggestion would be to look at cumulative energy expenditure during a longer period of time, or even calculating it using the two days presented in figure S9.
5. Overall, and related to the previous points, the authors claim in different parts of the manuscript that weight loss is observed with no changes in food intake or energy expenditure. It would be of importance that the authors could address better this question, with (as suggested above) prolonged measurements and if the phenotype holds, maybe look into absorption/intestinal issues that SGC707, for example, or any other model used might be inducing.
6. In relation to the titles of the first section of the paper (as well as the text), the authors claim that “Mono and Asymemetric (…) in correlation with feeding cycles” and in the second section the authors claim “PRMT3 Regulates Adipose ADMA during Feeding in an Insulin-pAKT-Dependent Manner”. Both in figure 1 and in figure 2 there is no particular experiment that shows that changes in ADMA or MMA levels are conneted to feeding behavior itself. Especially in figure 1, the experiments done show that there seems to exist in fact a circadian variantion in the level of these proteins, that might in fact mirror or be dependent on feeding/nutritional levels, but no experiments were done at this point to make such claims only with correlational data. I would suggest changing the claim according to the data presented where in figure 1 its possible to observe diurnal/nocturnal variations that might be circadian in nature and in figure 2 the changes with fasting might be correlated with fasting/lack of nutrition and not “feeding” as the title implies.
7. Also regarding the text on these sections, I would strongly recommend changing the first narrative, where the authors claim that the patterns observed mirror the feeding patterns of mice. Although it is true, that these changes to mirror the feeding patterns of animals on HFD, they also might mirror the sleeping patterns, locomotion patters, among other behaviors that take place during night time when the animals are active. I totally understand that it is part of constructing the narrative, but it is of my personal opinion that data should be the driver in these circumstances, and the data presented in the first sections does not allow for any conclusion on what is driving the observations.
And some additional comments that, although not major, are of some importance to the quality of the present work:
8. Time restricted feeding lowers Slc25a1 levels in WAT while the levels in the liver remain unchanged. To tackle how the changes in Slc25a1 affect the metabolic status of the animal, the authors created a mouse model that expresses the Cre recombinase under the Adiponectin promoter, assuring that the expression of Cre is restricted to adipocytes. To ensure that this deletion is specific to WAT (following the rationale of the paper where most changes in PRMT3 are seen in WAT), BAT data on figure 6d should be added.
9. Regarding figure 2, as it has been repeatidely described in the literature, that prolonged fasting decreases phosphorylation levels of AKT, as shown for example in figure 2r. Unfortunately, in figure 2j and 2l the levels of pAKT presented seem to be quite elevated for a 36h fast. On top, a ratio of pAKT/AKT is not present and AKT levels are not shown in figure 2j. In figure 3 the legend claims that WB were performed in 12week old animals upon 36h of fasting. With all conditions being equal, it would be important to address the differences in pAKT levels and also include a pAKT/AKT ratio.
10. The overexpression model does not seem to answer any particular question and does’t seem to add any particular insight into the question tackled in this current manuscript. If the authors want to use the overexpression model, it would be ideal at least to show that the over expression worked, since it seems to have an effect on glucose levels homeostasis.
11. A slightly minor comment (and surely irrelevant for the revision process) but, regarding some of the wording used, the expression “time-restricted feeding” is more commonly used than the expression “time-restricted fasting”.
12. I would strongly recommend further proof reading since some words seem to be missplaced, as for example in line 330 the authors write “primarily due to a decrease in liver mass”. Looking at the figure, I would imagine that the authors probably were referring to lean mass.

(C, D) Body weight (C) and food intake (D) of the mice. (E-G) VO2 (E), heat production (F) and RER (G) of the mice as measured by a metabolic chamber. (H) Glucose concentrations during GTT and AUC.
4. Regarding the regulation of SLC25A1 by PRMT3. The expression pattern of SLC25A1 in response to the feeding cycle is interesting. Although this change mirrors the changes of PRMT3, whether there is a direct causative relationship is not addressed. Also, the rationale for focusing on SLC25A1 as the downstream target of PRMT3 is not strong. They mentioned a previous publication regarding SLC25A1 interaction with PRMT3 and PRMT5. This paper was not cited.
Authors’ response: Thanks for the comments. We have now cited the reference that indicates the interaction between PRMT3 and SLC25A1 (4).
The authors suggested that PRMT3 might methylate SLC25A1 or at least regulate SCL25A1 methylation. This needs to be thoroughly characterized, including the sites of methylation on SLC25A1, and how methylation may directly affect SLC25A1 protein level.
Authors’ response: We have now identified that R282 and R285 of SLC25A1, which were located in the citrate binding region of SLC25A1, were the methylation sites (Figure R7A, B). Mutation of R282G and R285C (SLC25A1Mut) reduced the interface area of the SLC25A1 protein (Figure R7B). Co-IP experiments in 293T cells transfected with PRMT3 and SLC25A1WT/SLC25A1Mut confirmed that SLC25A1 mutation reduced its methylation (Figure R7C). Further, the anti-ADMA antibody successfully pulled down SLC25A1WT but not SLC25A1Mut, indicating that R282 and R285 were the asymmetrically di-methylated arginine residues of SLC25A1 (Figure R7D). In addition, Co-IP experiments demonstrated that the interaction between PRMT3 and SLC25A1 was weakened after mutation (Figure R7E). We then performed a CHX assay to assess the effects of SLC25A1 arginine methylation on its protein stability. The results showed that PRMT3 could stabilise the SLC25A1 protein in a methylation-dependent manner (Figure R7F, G). These data have been added to Fig.4f-l of the revised manuscript.
Figure. R7 (A) Protein sequence alignment of SLC25A1 from Drosophila melanogaster to Homo sapiens indicating the conserved R282 and R285 sites. (B) Structural prediction of WT SLC25A1 (SLC25A1WT) and R282G/R285C (SLC25A1Mut) by AlphaFold 3. (C) IP of FLAG in 293T cells transfected with PRMT3 and SLC25A1WT/SLC25A1Mut and WB of ADMA confirmed that SLC25A1 mutation reduced its methylation. (D) IP of ADMA in 293T cells transfected with PRMT3 and SLC25A1WT/SLC25A1Mut and WB of FLAG confirmed that SLC25A1 mutation reduced its methylation. (E) IP of FLAG in 293T cells transfected with PRMT3 and SLC25A1WT/SLC25A1Mut and WB of MYC confirmed that SLC25A1 mutation reduced its interaction with PRMT3. (F, G) Protein stability of SLC25A1WT and SLC25A1Mut with or without PRMT3 by CHX assay.
Additionally, the authors suggest that SLC25A1 expression is also regulated by the insulin-AKT pathway (Fig. 4p). Is this through PRMT3?
Authors’ response: We have now shown that insulin increased the levels of SLC25A1 under fasting but not in the presence of SGC707 (Figure R8A, B), indicating the Insulin-pAKT was the upstream regulator of SLC25A1 through PRMT3. This data has been added in Fig. 5o, p of the revised manuscript.
Figure. R8 (A, B) Western blot analysis (A) and quantification (B) of SLC25A1 in eWAT at fasted for 36 h (Ctrl), fasted for 36 h, then treated with insulin via intraperitoneal injection for 3 h (Insulin) or fasted for 36 h then treated with insulin plus SGC707 (Insulin+SGC707).
Lastly, what contributes to the tissue-specific regulation of PRMT3 and SLC25A1 in eWAT, but not in other adipose tissues?
Authors’ response: We found that injection of CL316,243, which is a β3-adrenoceptor agonist, reduced the levels of PRMT3 and SLC25A1 in eWAT, but not BAT and liver. Moreover, the effect was similar to that of fasting (Figure R9A, B). CL316,243 is an effective stimulant of adipocyte lipolysis and increments of pHSL660 were observed in eWAT after fasting or CL316,243 treatment.
Figure. R9 (A, B) Western blot analysis (A) and quantification (B) of SLC25A1 and PRMT3 in eWAT, BAT and Liver of 12 weeks old male B6N mice at ad libitum (Fed), fasted for 36 h, ad libitum with PBS (Fed+ PBS) or CL316,243 (Fed+ CL316,243) via intraperitoneal injection.
In addition, in cultured adipocytes derived from mouse eWAT (SVF), enhancement of adipocyte lipolysis by CL316,243 or Norepinephrine treatment also decreased the levels of PRMT3 and SLC25A1 (Figure R10A, B), raising the possibility that adipocyte lipolysis may contribute to the tissue-specific regulation of PRMT3 and SLC25A1. This hypothesis will be further tested in our following study.
Figure. R10 (A) Western blot analysis of PRMT3 and SLC25A1 in cultured adipocyte differentiated from eWAT-derived SVF cells with or without CL316,243 treatment. (B) Western blot analysis of PRMT3 a in cultured adipocyte differentiated from eWAT-derived SVF cells with or without Norepinephrine treatment.
5. Although PRMT3 inhibition by SGC707 and adipocyte-specific knockout of SLC25A1 both reduce diet-induced obesity, the extent to which PRMT3-mediated SLC25A1 methylation contributes to this process is not clear. For example, will supplement the expression of SLC25A1 in PRMT3 KO restores some of the metabolic features? Similarly, what happens if applying SGC707 on SCL25A1 conditional knockout mouse model? It is more convincing that SLC25A1 expression changes in response to feeding, whereas changes in PRMT3 are rather minor.
Authors’ response: We have now treated WT and Slc25a1AKO mice with SGC707. The results indicated that there were no additional effects in the glucose sensitivities with/without either SLC25A1 or SGC707. Thus, the PRMT3-mediated SLC25A1 methylation contributes to improved glucose metabolism.
Figure. R11 (A, B) Blood glucose levels (A) and area under the curve (AUC) (B) of male WT and Slc25a1AKO mice during glucose tolerance test after 10 weeks of HFD with or without SGC707 treatment.
6. Page 9, section title “TRF reduces PRMT3-SLC25A1 interaction…” was not supported by the data shown in Fig. 5.
Authors’ response: Thanks for the suggestion. We have corrected it into ‘Time-Restricted Fasting Reduces PRMT3/SLC25A1 levels and Ameliorates Diet-Induced Obesity’ in the revised manuscript.
Other critiques
1. The authors use recombinant proteins to test the specificity of PRMT3 antibody. This method is not appropriate. They should use PRMT3 knockout cell lines to confirm that the signal they see with the antibody is indeed PRMT3 (PRMT3 knockout cells are viable). In many cases, the changes of PRMT3 protein levels are very marginal (eg. Fig. 2b, 2f, 2j, 2l, Fig. 3r, Fig. 5a).
Authors’ response: Thanks for the comment. As shown above in Figure. R6B, we have now included an AAV-mediated adipocyte-specific Prmt3 knockdown (KD) to validate the specificity of the antibody further.
2. The correlation between methylation levels and BMI is weak.
Authors’ response: Thanks for the suggestion. Although the current study found a significant correlation between methylation levels and BMI, we would like to include more human samples in the future to enhance the statistical power.
Reference #1
1. Choi, S., Choi, D., Lee, Y. K., Ahn, S. H., Seong, J. K., Chi, S. W., ... & Koo, S. H. (2021). Depletion of Prmt1 in adipocytes impairs glucose homeostasis in diet-induced obesity. Diabetes, 70(8), 1664-1678.
2. Capelo-Diz, A., Lachiondo-Ortega, S., Fernández-Ramos, D., Cañas-Martín, J., Goikoetxea-Usandizaga, N., Serrano-Maciá, M., ... & Varela-Rey, M. (2023). Hepatic levels of S-adenosylmethionine regulate the adaptive response to fasting. Cell Metabolism, 35(8), 1373-1389.
3. de Jong, L. M., Zhang, Z., den Hartog, Y., Sijsenaar, T. J., Martins Cardoso, R., Manson, M. L., ... & Hoekstra, M. (2022). PRMT3 inhibitor SGC707 reduces triglyceride levels and induces pruritus in Western-type diet-fed LDL receptor knockout mice. Scientific Reports, 12(1), 483.
4. Wei, H. H., Fan, X. J., Hu, Y., Tian, X. X., Guo, M., Mao, M. W., ... & Wang, Z. (2021). A systematic survey of PRMT interactomes reveals the key roles of arginine methylation in the global control of RNA splicing and translation. Science Bulletin, 66(13), 1342-1357.
Reviewer #2 (Remarks to the Author):
In this manuscript the authors study how different dietary approaches change levels of PRMT3 and MMA/ADMA in white adipose tissue (WAT). In WAT, the authors firstly show a circadian regulation of MMA/ADMA levels, which seems to be abrogated upon HFD. Furthermore, inhibition of PRMT3 by SGC707 reverts weight gain on a HFD as well as it accelerates the decrease of MMA/ADMA levels during a 12h fast to levels similar to a 36h fast, on an insulin dependant way. The authors also claim that SLC25a1 is implicated. Besides the role of PRMT3 in the levels of MMA/ADMA, the authors study the changes in these proteins using a Time Restricted Feeding (TRF) paradigm and draw a parallel between TRF and SGC707 action upon long term HFD consumption.
Former studies have implicated PRMT3/SGC707 in weight loss and ameliorated phenotype from liver steatosis, also showing an improvement on overall WAT morphology. Overall, literature on PRMT3 or its inhibitor is lacking in models of HFD, and its effects on body weight, although known, are still quite understudied. This adds to the novelty of this present study.
Regarding the study itself, in my opinion, some major considerations are as follows:
1. In figure 1c the authors claim that animals on HFD showed a “marked increase” in proteins containing MMA and ADMA. HFD feeding is known to alter several parameters that have a circadian component to it as well as feeding patterns. As such, one can wonder whether the time of collecting the tissue can have an impact on MMA and ADMA levels, and whether repeating the experiment done on figure 1a would help to get a better understanding on whether this changes in protein level are continuous during a 24h period or shifted in comparison to NCD. In my opinion, this experiment has relevance towards the claim of the paper, since understanding the dynamics of protein levels both in NCD as in HFD could influence the timing of fasting for improved outcomes.
Authors’ response: Thanks for the suggestion. We have now performed time-course sampling for HFD, and added data showing that the circadian patterns of ADMA, PRMT3 and SLC25A1 during 24 hours disappeared after HFD (Figure R12A, B). This data has been added to Fig. S1f of the revised manuscript.
Figure. R12 (A) Western blot analysis (A) and quantification (B) of proteins carrying ADMA, SLC25A1 and PRMT3 in eWAT of DIO mice sacrificed at the indicated time points in a 12-hour light/dark cycle (n = 4).
2. In figure 2, the authors show that a 12h fast in addition to the administration of SGC mimics the results of a 36h fasting, regarding MMA and ADMA levels. This experiment is central to the claim of the paper, since one of the main premisses is that by inhibiting PRMT3 during a 12h the observed decrease in MMA and ADMA levels is similar to a 36h fast. It is of my opinion that is highly important to also show that, in this particular experiment (figure 2h and 2i) the levels of ADMA and MMA in ad libitum animals administered the drug remain unchanged. In this way its possible to ensure that proper controls are in place.
Authors’ response: Thank you for the suggestion. We have supplemented the data from ad libitum animals administered SGC707. The result showed that the inhibition of PRMT3 by SGC707 did not change the ADMA level in ad libitum animals (Figure R13A, B). This data has been added to Fig. S4a, b of the revised manuscript.
Figure. R13 (A) Western blot analysis (A) and quantification (B) of proteins carrying ADMA in eWAT of mice at ad libitum (Fed) and ad libitum with SGC707 via intraperitoneal injection.
3. The authors present data on the effects of PRMT3 inhibition in overall metabolism and body mass. The authors claim that no changes in food intake nor energy expenditure were observed on a 24h period. 24h readings can be misleading as small incremental changes can be observed when measures are taking for extended periods of time. A prolonged measurement entailing 5-7 days would allow for a better overview and a more convincing claim that the weight loss is not due to small cumulative changes in feeding amounts/energy expenditure. A longer assessment of the RER could also provide better proof that this delta RER changes are repeated daily in prolonged periods and not on a particular single isolated event.
Authors’ response: Thank you for your comment. Based on these suggestions, we have placed the SGC707-treated mice in a metabolic chamber for continuous observation over 7 days. The results showed that there was a slight increase in energy expenditure, especially at night time (Figure R14A), which was also aligned with the increased RER at night time. There was also no difference in the average food intake of the mice (Figure R14B). The daily changes in delta RER were repeatable in the prolonged periods (Figure R14C). These data have been added to Fig. S7e-h of the revised manuscript.
Figure. R14 (A) energy expenditure as indicated by heat production (kcal/hr) was measured in a metabolic chamber for 7 continuous days, and the average night heat production was quantified. (B) Average food intake of the mice. (C) RER was measured in a metabolic chamber for 7 continuous days, and the average delta RER level was measured.
4. It has been published that TRF changes body weight without affecting total caloric intake, and the authors are able to replicate this finding. Furthermore, in figure S9m, we can observe an increase in locomotion during the night cycle, which also goes with current literature. In this present study, we observe changes in body weight in HFD animals under a TRF paradigm, without alteration of food intake or energy expenditure (Figure S9). It would be important for the authors to adress this particular data set, where increased locomotion but unchanged energy expenditure and feeding behaviour are observed. An important suggestion would be to look at cumulative energy expenditure during a longer period of time, or even calculating it using the two days presented in figure S9.
Authors’ response: Thank you for the suggestion. We have now recalculated the data in Fig. S9, and the result shows that TRF increased energy expenditure at nighttime (Figure R15A, B), which is consistent with the increased locomotor activity. We have corrected that data in Fig. S10k of the revised manuscript.
` Figure. R15 (A) energy expenditure as indicated by heat production (kcal/hr) was measured after 16:8 TRF and the average night heat production was quantified (B).
5. Overall, and related to the previous points, the authors claim in different parts of the manuscript that weight loss is observed with no changes in food intake or energy expenditure. It would be of importance that the authors could address better this question, with (as suggested above) prolonged measurements and if the phenotype holds, maybe look into absorption/intestinal issues that SGC707, for example, or any other model used might be inducing.
Authors’ response: Thank you for the comments. Following your suggestions, we have re-analysed the data and added a metabolic chamber that has been tested for a prolonged period. The results indicated an increase in energy expenditure. We have corrected these points in the revised manuscript.
6. In relation to the titles of the first section of the paper (as well as the text), the authors claim that “Mono and Asymemetric (…) in correlation with feeding cycles” and in the second section the authors claim “PRMT3 Regulates Adipose ADMA during Feeding in an Insulin-pAKT-Dependent Manner”. Both in figure 1 and in figure 2 there is no particular experiment that shows that changes in ADMA or MMA levels are conneted to feeding behavior itself. Especially in figure 1, the experiments done show that there seems to exist in fact a circadian variantion in the level of these proteins, that might in fact mirror or be dependent on feeding/nutritional levels, but no experiments were done at this point to make such claims only with correlational data. I would suggest changing the claim according to the data presented where in figure 1 its possible to observe diurnal/nocturnal variations that might be circadian in nature and in figure 2 the changes with fasting might be correlated with fasting/lack of nutrition and not “feeding” as the title implies.
Authors’ response: Thanks for the suggestions. We have changed Figure 1 into a diurnal expression pattern and Figure 2 into fasting, respectively. We have also changed the “feeding” in the title to “fasting”.
7. Also regarding the text on these sections, I would strongly recommend changing the first narrative, where the authors claim that the patterns observed mirror the feeding patterns of mice. Although it is true, that these changes to mirror the feeding patterns of animals on HFD, they also might mirror the sleeping patterns, locomotion patters, among other behaviors that take place during night time when the animals are active. I totally understand that it is part of constructing the narrative, but it is of my personal opinion that data should be the driver in these circumstances, and the data presented in the first sections does not allow for any conclusion on what is driving the observations.
Authors’ response: Thanks for the suggestions. We have changed the description that the patterns observed mirror the feeding patterns of mice into a diurnal expression pattern in the first section.
And some additional comments that, although not major, are of some importance to the quality of the present work:
8. Time restricted feeding lowers Slc25a1 levels in WAT while the levels in the liver remain unchanged. To tackle how the changes in Slc25a1 affect the metabolic status of the animal, the authors created a mouse model that expresses the Cre recombinase under the Adiponectin promoter, assuring that the expression of Cre is restricted to adipocytes. To ensure that this deletion is specific to WAT (following the rationale of the paper where most changes in PRMT3 are seen in WAT), BAT data on figure 6d should be added.
Authors’ response: Thanks for the suggestions. The Adiponectin-cre is expressed in all mature adipocytes, including white and brown. Thus, SLC25A1 was also deleted in BAT (Figure R16). Though we only focused on the function of PRMT3-SLC25A1 in visceral adipose tissue, the role of SLC25A1 in brown adipocytes remains unknown and interesting. A recent work reported the function of ACLY in brown adipocytes, which is the downstream protein of SLC25A1. Future work generating a Ucp1-cre-driven Slc25a1 deletion model will better address this question.
Figure. R16 Western blot analysis of SLC25A1 from BAT of WT and Slc25a1AKO mice.
9. Regarding figure 2, as it has been repeatidely described in the literature, that prolonged fasting decreases phosphorylation levels of AKT, as shown for example in figure 2r. Unfortunately, in figure 2j and 2l the levels of pAKT presented seem to be quite elevated for a 36h fast. On top, a ratio of pAKT/AKT is not present and AKT levels are not shown in figure 2j. In figure 3 the legend claims that WB were performed in 12week old animals upon 36h of fasting. With all conditions being equal, it would be important to address the differences in pAKT levels and also include a pAKT/AKT ratio.
Authors’ response: Thanks for raising this concern. We have now included the tAKT band, as well as a calculation of the pAKT/AKT ratio (Figure R17), in Figures 2j and k of the revised manuscript. For Fig. 2l, since there was no AL control, the results make sense that the level of pAKT elevated after insulin treatment.
Figure R17 Quantification of pAKT/AKT ratio of Fig. 2j.
10. The overexpression model does not seem to answer any particular question and does’t seem to add any particular insight into the question tackled in this current manuscript. If the authors want to use the overexpression model, it would be ideal at least to show that the over expression worked, since it seems to have an effect on glucose levels homeostasis.
Authors’ response: We have deleted the part of Slc25a1 overexpression according to your suggestion.
11. A slightly minor comment (and surely irrelevant for the revision process) but, regarding some of the wording used, the expression “time-restricted feeding” is more commonly used than the expression “time-restricted fasting”.
Authors’ response: Thanks for the suggestion. We have corrected time-restricted fasting into time-restricted feeding in the revised manuscript.
12. I would strongly recommend further proof reading since some words seem to be missplaced, as for example in line 330 the authors write “primarily due to a decrease in liver mass”. Looking at the figure, I would imagine that the authors probably were referring to lean mass.
Authors’ response: Thank you for the suggestion. We have corrected the liver mass to lean mass. In addition, we have further examined the manuscript and corrected the typos and mistakes.

### Reviewer 1

I appreciate the authors’ efforts in addressing my comments and revise the manuscript. The study has been clearly improved. However, I still have some concerns about the characterization of SLC25A1 methylation by PRMT3 and extent to which reduced SLC25A1 protein level is responsible for the phenotypes associated with PRMT3 KO.
1. The sites of PRMT3-catalyzed SLC25A1 methylation were determined by using a pan-ADMA antibody. More rigor experiments should be done to define the sites. They should perform in vitro methylation assay using recombinant proteins and detect the methylation and loss of methylation with the mutants using an antibody-independent approach, such as fluorography.
2. The authors mutated the two candidate arginine methylation sites (R282 and R285) to Glycine (G) and Cystine (C) respectively. The underlying rationale for this mutation was not mentioned. Arginine is positively charged, and it is generally accepted that R-to-K (lysine) is the proper way to introduce arginine methylation deficiency while maintain the positive charge of arginine. The G or C mutation may cause structural changes that could lead to protein misfolding, thus indirectly affect methylation.
3. As I mentioned in previous critiques, it is important to define the extent to which reduced SLC25A1 is responsible for PRMT3 KO phenotype. The authors should supplement/add back SLC25A1 in PRMT3 KO background and assess if it restores functional impact of PRMT3 KO.

### Reviewer 2

After carefully reviewing the updated manuscript, I find that the authors have satisfactorily addressed all the points raised during the first round of revisions.
I would only suggest, since I am confident that the data is available from the metabolic studies, that the authors provide a cumulative curve of food intake over a period longer than 24 hours. This would help confirm that the drug does not have a small yet cumulative effect on food intake.
Including this analysis would reinforce the central claim of the paper.
